> TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8

I know it's customary for HN to edit titles to remove extraneous information, but removing "Linux" here really takes away something useful and relevant. This is a Linux vulnerability. If you're running *BSD or Mac or Windows, not affected.

Here's the NIST link: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-98432

Here are my notes so far after digging into this with Claude + defensive access:

1. Not just an MPTCP thing - any received IPv4 packet with options creates the problematic conditions.

2. Also appears that using NetLabel/CIPSO (SELinux or Smack with a CIPSOV4 mapping) creates the same conditions that a packet with IP options would. If you're using these, it might mean that dropping IPv4 packets with IP options might not fully mitigate.

3. At least for our test VMs in Azure (accelerated networking) I wasn't able to get any IPv4 packets with options through, from three different US-based ISPs. Unfortunately Microsoft publishes no docs on whether the fabric drops this or not, so YMMV.

We're using a simple XDP program to mitigate until a patched kernel is available (thanks @tptacek for the idea):

https://github.com/jamilbk/drop-ipv4-opt

Some notes I've got about this:

- MPTCP is not a requirement, it is a generic use-after-free.

- Exploitability over the internet is unlikely, most ISP routers drop packets with IP options fields.

- At least according to Red Hat, dropping packets with IP options yourself helps, but is not a full mitigation.

- Successful exploit requires multiple CPU cores to process packets, so systems with just a single core or packet processing pinned to a single core are not affected.

The difference between now and next year is that we won’t have time next year to patch before malicious agents use this exploit against everything at lighting speed. Global internet downtime will be the only solution.
